title: Federal Travel Regulation; Reorganizing and Streamlining the Federal Travel Regulation To Improve Operational Efficiency
summary:
The General Services Administration just issued a sweeping rewrite of the Federal Travel Regulation to streamline how the government manages official travel and employee relocations. The rule shifts the entire rulebook to a clearer, narrative format, trims redundant text, and gives agencies more flexibility, with the goal of cutting administrative effort and saving taxpayer dollars. It takes effect December 8, 2025.

Structurally, the regulation is reorganized so that one chapter is now a simple glossary, while other chapters focus on travel, relocation, death-related benefits, and situations where outside groups can pay for government travel. The overall length is cut by nearly half, and the agency estimates a 10‑year net cost avoidance of roughly $650,000 from reduced time spent navigating the rules. The rewrite supports a broader deregulatory push and was found not to be a “major rule” for Congressional review.

For federal travelers, several changes matter day to day. Agencies choose the most advantageous travel method without a preset pecking order, and the rules keep familiar programs like government airline fares and the requirement to use U.S. carriers when applicable. Meal reimbursements are simpler when a provided meal can’t be eaten for medical or religious reasons, and “laundry” is no longer listed as its own category, which may prompt agencies to address it within general miscellaneous expenses policies. Conference planning guidance is removed from the regulation, with agencies expected to issue their own direction. For temporary quarters during moves, the government eliminates the “actual” and “lump-sum” methods and uses a single “lodgings‑plus” method to reduce paperwork. And for home purchases at a new duty station, agencies may now reimburse buyer broker fees and real estate commissions, making it easier for relocating employees to use a buyer’s agent.

Other clarifications include rules for families where two members are both federal employees, renewed tours in Alaska and Hawaii, and consistent definitions of “immediate family” across emergency and law enforcement protections. The rule also removes the governmentwide requirement for agencies to submit an annual report on first and business class airline use, arguing that such trips are rare and can be overseen internally, while keeping the strict limits on when premium seating is allowed.

Who stands to benefit? Agencies and travelers should find a leaner, clearer rulebook, faster decisions, and less time spent on paperwork. Employees relocating may gain from simpler temporary quarters rules and the ability to be reimbursed for buyer broker fees. Taxpayers may see modest savings from reduced administrative burden.

Who might see downsides? Watchdogs and transparency advocates may be concerned about dropping the annual premium‑class reporting requirement. Employees who preferred a lump‑sum option for temporary quarters could lose flexibility. More discretion at the agency level may mean less consistency across government. And by reverting older language that is neutral about vehicle types, the rule walks back an earlier push that some saw as encouraging alternative‑fuel use.

Overall, this is a broad modernization aimed at clarity and efficiency, with some tradeoffs in standardization and reporting.
